title: The if-something-happens-to-me file: where to start
dek: Give someone a way to find the right people, papers and household details without putting every secret in one folder. Start with one useful page.
metaDescription: Build an if-something-happens-to-me file with document locations, trusted contacts and household instructions. Keep access separate from authority.

sources.name: CaringInfo: advance directives by state and territory
sources.note: Advance-directive forms and requirements depend on location. An information file does not replace the appropriate legal documents.

paragraphs: An if-something-happens-to-me file is a map of important people, documents, accounts and household responsibilities. It tells an appropriate person what exists, where to look and whom to call. It does not give that person legal authority, change who inherits, or replace a will, power of attorney or health-care directive.

The question is smaller than sorting your entire life: if you could not explain things tomorrow, where would someone start? Not every account number. Not every password. Just enough accurate directions to stop the first person helping you from searching every drawer.

This guide is for adults preparing practical information for illness, incapacity or death. Legal authority, privacy and document requirements depend on the situation and location. Ask a qualified professional about the documents you need rather than treating this folder as a legal plan.

body.heading: Make a useful first page
items: Choose who should know that the file exists, and ask whether they are willing to help. Do not assume a relative can or wants to take on every task.
Write the location of your current legal documents and the professional or office to contact. Identify originals separately from copies.
List immediate responsibilities: dependent care, pets, essential household services, keys and any safety or access information that cannot wait.
Add the institutions where accounts and policies exist, using enough detail to identify them without exposing unnecessary credentials.
Date the page, choose a protected storage location and explain how the appropriate person can find it when needed.

body.heading: What belongs in the file, and what belongs elsewhere
rows: Who to contact and what role they have agreed to
Document type, location of the original and relevant professional
The originals, stored according to professional guidance
Institution, policy type and contact route
Passwords, recovery codes and full identity details
Essential contacts, responsibilities and where instructions are kept
Keys, access codes and other security information
Which account or provider has an approved legacy or recovery process
A plain-text master list of credentials accessible to everyone

body.heading: Finding a document is not the same as being allowed to act
paragraphs: Someone may know where an account is without being authorised to use it. A person named in a will may still need to follow the appropriate estate process. A person who helps with bills while you are well may not have the authority required if you lose capacity. Keep these questions separate from the practical question of where the paperwork lives.

For health-care preferences, [CaringInfo's state and territory resources](https://www.caringinfo.org/planning/advance-directives/) provide a starting point for the relevant advance-directive forms. Read the instructions for your location. An informal note about your wishes may help a conversation, but do not label it a legally effective directive without checking the requirements.

Use the [emergency contact and medical decision-maker guide](/guides/emergency-contact-and-medical-decision-maker) to distinguish being reachable from being authorised. If family circumstances, property ownership or legal arrangements are complicated, get professional advice before promising someone a role.

body.heading: A first version that is small enough to finish
paragraphs: An invented example: Maya writes that the originals of her legal documents are with a named professional, the household folder is in the locked cabinet, and her sister knows the agreed access process. She lists the mortgage provider and insurer by name, not their passwords. She adds the contact for the person who can collect her child under the school's current arrangements.

That is not a complete estate or emergency plan. It is a starting point someone can follow. The next pass adds other institutions and responsibilities. The file distinguishes an agreed role from a person Maya still needs to ask, and it dates every section so a helper can spot older information.

body.heading: Have the conversation before the folder is needed

items.line: I am making a short record of where important things are. Would you be willing to know where it is and who to contact? That does not mean you are agreeing to manage everything.
I have listed where the documents are, but I want to check who may act and when. Which documents and access arrangements are appropriate for this situation?

body.heading: Check the file after a meaningful change
items: Update contact details and document locations after a move, relationship change, new dependent or changed professional adviser.
Replace superseded directions clearly rather than leaving conflicting versions in several folders.
Review access after changing a lock, device, provider or security arrangement. Do not solve access by distributing credentials indiscriminately.
Ask the appropriate person whether the directions are understandable. They should be able to locate a named document without you giving a second set of instructions.

items.q: Is an if-something-happens-to-me file the same as a will?
items.a: No. It is an information and location record. A will and other legal arrangements serve different purposes and must meet applicable requirements. Keep the location of current documents in the file, but get professional advice about their legal effect and who has authority to act.

items.q: Should I put every password in the folder?
items.a: Not as an openly accessible list. Record where approved access or recovery arrangements are managed, and protect credentials according to the relevant provider and security guidance. The appropriate process may differ during incapacity and after death. Knowing that an account exists does not authorise someone to sign in.

items.q: Is a half-finished file worth keeping?
items.a: Yes, if it clearly says what is current, what is incomplete and where the information came from. Start with immediate responsibilities and key document locations. Do not present an unfinished list as a complete legal or financial inventory, and avoid leaving a confident-looking answer where the real answer is unknown.

body.heading: Keep the map usable
paragraphs: The best first file is not the thickest one. It is the one with accurate directions, a clear access plan and someone who knows it exists. For the broader checklist, use [what to write down in case something happens](/guides/what-to-write-down-in-case-something-happens-to-you).

[Personal Life Affairs Companion](/shop/personal-life-affairs-companion) is an optional way to organise information you choose to record. It does not turn an information file into a will or grant authority. A protected folder and the free worksheet here are enough to begin.
